name: Captain Lakshmi Sahgal
tagline: The doctor who traded her stethoscope for a revolution
story:
In 1943, a young Indian doctor named Lakshmi Swaminathan stood in a crowded hall in Burma, listening to Subhas Chandra Bose call for soldiers to free India from British rule. She had built a comfortable medical practice treating Indian laborers in Malaya. She had everything to lose. But when Bose asked who would lead an all-women regiment — the first of its kind in Asian history — Lakshmi stepped forward without hesitation. She was 28.

As Captain of the Rani of Jhansi Regiment, she trained 1,500 women who had never held a weapon into a disciplined fighting force. They marched through jungle, monsoon, and starvation toward the Indian border. When the campaign collapsed under Allied counterattack, Lakshmi refused to flee. She stayed behind to tend to wounded soldiers until she was captured by the British in 1945. At her trial, the prosecution called her a traitor. The Indian public called her a hero.

After independence, most would have rested on that legacy. Lakshmi went back to medicine. She opened a clinic in Kanpur that treated the poorest patients for free — for over fifty years. She never stopped. At 88, she ran for President of India. At 97, she was still seeing patients. When asked why she never retired, she said simply: "There is always someone who needs help."

Captain Lakshmi Sahgal proved that grit isn't one dramatic moment — it's a lifetime of refusing to stop when the world gives you every reason to.
